content.title: About
content.content: Irish soda bread is a traditional quick‑bread made from wheat flour, baking soda, buttermilk (or kefir) and salt. The alkaline soda reacts with the acidic dairy to leaven the dough, so the loaf is ready in 30–45 minutes. It has a dense yet slightly moist crumb, a mild tangy flavor and a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bread originated in the 19th century as a fast‑baking solution when yeast was scarce.
Traditional recipes use buttermilk or kefir, giving the loaf its characteristic subtle sour note.
In Ireland it is commonly served with butter and jam, and used as a base for hearty sandwiches.
Baking soda replaces yeast, allowing the bread to stay soft without a long rise.
In the United States the same style is known as “soda bread” and became popular among immigrants in the early 20th century.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides sustained energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains calcium and phosphorus
items.content: The dairy component adds minerals important for bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, soda bread contains little fat when no butter is added.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Quick and easy to make
items.content: No yeast means less time and energy spent, making it convenient for busy lifestyles.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, so the bread is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rapidly digestible carbs can raise blood sugar, which should be considered by diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The added salt may be a concern for those monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soda bread is delicious fresh, lightly toasted with butter, cheese or jam. It works well as a base for open‑face sandwiches, as croutons in soups, and alongside traditional Irish dishes such as stewed cabbage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or cloth wrap at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, wrap tightly in plastic and refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Warm in the oven before serving to restore a crisp crust.
